The [states](U.S._states "U.S. states") and territories included in the [United States Census Bureau](United_States_Census_Bureau "United States Census Bureau")'s statistics for the United States population, ethnicity, religion, and most other categories include the [50 states](U.S._state "U.S. state") and [Washington, D.C.](Washington%2C_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") Separate statistics are maintained for the five permanently inhabited [territories of the United States](Territories_of_the_United_States "Territories of the United States"): [Puerto Rico](Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), <Guam>, the [U.S. Virgin Islands](U.S._Virgin_Islands "U.S. Virgin Islands"), [American Samoa](American_Samoa "American Samoa"), and the [Northern Mariana Islands](Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands").[[1]](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-1)

As of April 1, 2010, the date of the [2010 United States Census](2010_United_States_Census "2010 United States Census"), the nine most populous [U.S. states](U.S._state "U.S. state") contain slightly more than half of the total population. The 25 least populous states contain less than one-sixth of the total population. <California>, the most populous state, contains more people than the 21 least populous states combined, and <Wyoming>, the least populous state, has a population less than any of the 31 [most populous U.S.](List_of_United_States_cities_by_population "List of United States cities by population") [cities](City "City").

## Method

The [United States Census](United_States_Census "United States Census") counts the persons residing in the [United States](United_States "United States") including [citizens](Citizenship "Citizenship"), non-citizen [permanent residents](Permanent_residence_(United_States) "Permanent residence (United States)") and non-citizen long-term visitors.[[2]](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-2) Civilian and military federal employees serving abroad and their dependents are counted in their home state.[[3]](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-3)

## Electoral apportionment

Every 10 years, the [U.S. Census Bureau](U.S._Census_Bureau "U.S. Census Bureau") is charged with making an actual count of all residents by state and territory. The accuracy of this count is then tested after the fact, and sometimes statistically significant undercounts or overcounts occur. For example for the [2020 decennial census](2020_United_States_census "2020 United States census"), 14 states had significant miscounts ranging from 1.5% to 6.6%. While these adjustments may be reflected in government programs over the following decade, the 10-year representative apportionments discussed below are not changed to reflect the miscount.[[4]](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-4)

### House of Representatives

Based on this decennial census, each state is allocated a portion of the 435 fixed seats in the [United States House of Representatives](United_States_House_of_Representatives "United States House of Representatives") (until the early 20th century, the apportionment process generally increased the size of the House based on the results of the census until the size of the House was capped by the [Reapportionment Act of 1929](Reapportionment_Act_of_1929 "Reapportionment Act of 1929")), with each state guaranteed at least one Representative. The [allocation](United_States_congressional_apportionment "United States congressional apportionment") is based on each state's proportion of the combined population of the [fifty states](U.S._state "U.S. state") (not including the [District of Columbia](District_of_Columbia "District of Columbia"), <Guam>, [American Samoa](American_Samoa "American Samoa"), the [Northern Mariana Islands](Northern_Mariana_Islands "Northern Mariana Islands"), [Puerto Rico](Puerto_Rico "Puerto Rico"), or the [United States Virgin Islands](United_States_Virgin_Islands "United States Virgin Islands")).

### Electoral College

The [Electoral College](Electoral_College_(United_States) "Electoral College (United States)"), every four years, elects the [President](President_of_the_United_States "President of the United States") and [Vice President of the United States](Vice_President_of_the_United_States "Vice President of the United States") based on the popular vote in each state and the District of Columbia. Each state's number of votes in the Electoral College is equal to its number of members in the Senate plus members in the House of Representatives.[[5]](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population#cite_note-auto-5)

## Etymology

Main articles: [Etymology of California](Etymology_of_California "Etymology of California") and [Island of California](Island_of_California "Island of California")

The Spaniards gave the name *Las Californias* to the peninsula of Baja California and to Alta California, the latter region becoming the present-day state of California.

The name derived from the mythical island of California in the fictional story of [Queen Calafia](Calafia "Calafia"), as recorded in a 1510 work *[The Adventures of Esplandián](Las_sergas_de_Esplandi%C3%A1n "Las sergas de Esplandián")* by [Castilian](Castilians "Castilians") author [Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo](Garci_Rodr%C3%ADguez_de_Montalvo "Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo").[[37]](California#cite_note-:1-39) This work was the fifth in a popular Spanish [chivalric romance](Chivalric_romance "Chivalric romance") series that began with *[Amadís de Gaula](Amad%C3%ADs_de_Gaula "Amadís de Gaula")*.[[38]](California#cite_note-Lavender_1987-40)[[39]](California#cite_note-41)[[40]](California#cite_note-42) Queen Calafia's kingdom was said to be a remote land rich in gold and pearls, inhabited by beautiful Black women who wore gold armor and lived like <Amazons>, as well as [griffins](Griffin "Griffin") and other strange beasts.[[37]](California#cite_note-:1-39)[[41]](California#cite_note-43)[[42]](California#cite_note-44) In the fictional paradise, the ruler Queen Calafia fought alongside Muslims and her name may have been chosen to echo the Muslim title [caliph](Caliph "Caliph"), used for Muslim leaders.[[37]](California#cite_note-:1-39)[[43]](California#cite_note-45)
> Know ye that at the right hand of the Indies there is an island called California, very close to that part of the Terrestrial Paradise, which was inhabited by black women without a single man among them, and they lived in the manner of Amazons. They were robust of body with strong passionate hearts and great virtue. The island itself is one of the wildest in the world on account of the bold and craggy rocks.
>
> — Chapter CLVII of *[The Adventures of Esplandián](Las_sergas_de_Esplandi%C3%A1n "Las sergas de Esplandián")*[[44]](California#cite_note-46)

In California, as of 2009, the [U.S. Department of Defense](U.S._Department_of_Defense "U.S. Department of Defense") had a total of 117,806 [active duty](Active_duty "Active duty") servicemembers of which 88,370 were [Sailors](United_States_Navy "United States Navy") or [Marines](United_States_Marine_Corps "United States Marine Corps"), 18,339 were [Airmen](United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force"), and 11,097 were [Soldiers](United_States_Army "United States Army"), with 61,365 Department of Defense civilian employees. In 2010, [Los Angeles County](Los_Angeles_County "Los Angeles County") was the largest origin of military recruits in the United States by county, with 1,437 individuals enlisting in the military.[[360]](California#cite_note-368) However, as of 2002, Californians were relatively under-represented in the military as a proportion to its population.[[361]](California#cite_note-369)

In 2000, California, had 2,569,340 veterans of United States [military service](Military_service "Military service"): 504,010 served in World War II, 301,034 in the [Korean War](Korean_War "Korean War"), 754,682 during the [Vietnam War](Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), and 278,003 during 1990–2000 (including the Persian Gulf War).[[362]](California#cite_note-City_Data_CA_Armed_Forces-370) As of 2010, there were 1,942,775 veterans living in California, of which 1,457,875 served during a period of armed conflict, and just over four thousand served [before World War II](Interwar_period "Interwar period") (the largest population of this group of any state).[[363]](California#cite_note-371)

California's military forces consist of the [Army and Air National Guard](California_National_Guard "California National Guard"), the [naval and state military reserve](California_State_Military_Reserve "California State Military Reserve") (militia), and the [California Cadet Corps](California_Cadet_Corps "California Cadet Corps").

On August 5, 1950, a [nuclear-capable](Silverplate "Silverplate") United States Air Force [Boeing B-29 Superfortress](Boeing_B-29_Superfortress "Boeing B-29 Superfortress") bomber carrying a [nuclear bomb](Mark_4_nuclear_bomb "Mark 4 nuclear bomb") crashed shortly after takeoff from [Fairfield-Suisun Air Force Base](Fairfield-Suisun_Air_Force_Base "Fairfield-Suisun Air Force Base"). sity of climate and terrain, the state has six life zones which are the lower [Sonoran Desert](Sonoran_Desert "Sonoran Desert"); upper Sonoran (foothill regions and some coastal lands), transition (coastal areas and moist northeastern counties); and the Canadian, Hudsonian, and Arctic Zones, comprising the state's highest elevations.[[168]](California#cite_note-California:_flora_and_fauna-170)

Plant life in the dry climate of the lower Sonoran zone contains a diversity of native cactus, mesquite, and paloverde. The [Joshua tree](Yucca_brevifolia "Yucca brevifolia") is found in the Mojave Desert. Flowering plants include the dwarf desert poppy and a variety of [asters](Aster_(genus) "Aster (genus)"). [Fremont cottonwood](Fremont_cottonwood "Fremont cottonwood") and [valley oak](Valley_oak "Valley oak") thrive in the Central Valley. The upper Sonoran zone includes the chaparral belt, characterized by forests of small shrubs, stunted trees, and herbaceous plants. *<Nemophila>*, [mint](Lamiaceae "Lamiaceae"), *<Phacelia>*, *[Viola](Viola_(plant) "Viola (plant)")*, and the California poppy (*[Eschscholzia californica](Eschscholzia_californica "Eschscholzia californica")*, the state flower) also flourish in this zone, along with the lupine, more species of which occur here than anywhere else in the world.[[168]](California#cite_note-California:_flora_and_fauna-170)

The transition zone includes most of California's forests with the redwood (*[Sequoia sempervirens](Sequoia_sempervirens "Sequoia sempervirens")*) and the "big tree" or giant sequoia (*[Sequoiadendron giganteum](Sequoiadendron_giganteum "Sequoiadendron giganteum")*), among the oldest living things on earth (some are said to have lived at least 4,000 years). [Tanbark oak](Tanbark_oak "Tanbark oak"), [California laurel](California_laurel "California laurel"), [sugar pine](Sugar_pine "Sugar pine"), [madrona](Arbutus "Arbutus"), [broad-leaved maple](Acer_macrophyllum "Acer macrophyllum"), and <Douglas-fir> also grow here. Forest floors are covered with [swordfern](Polystichum "Polystichum"), alumnroot, [barrenwort](Barrenwort "Barrenwort"), and [trillium](Trillium "Trillium"), and there are thickets of [huckleberry](Huckleberry "Huckleberry"), [azalea](Azalea "Azalea"), elder, and wild currant. Characteristic wild flowers include varieties of mariposa, [tulip](Tulip "Tulip"), and [tiger](Lilium_columbianum "Lilium columbianum") and [leopard](Lilium_pardalinum "Lilium pardalinum") lilies.[[169]](California#cite_note-Sequoia_sempervirens_(D._Don)_Endl.-171)

The high elevations of the Canadian zone allow the [Jeffrey pine](Jeffrey_pine "Jeffrey pine"), [red fir](Red_fir "Red fir"), and [lodgepole pine](Lodgepole_pine "Lodgepole pine") to thrive. Brushy areas are abundant with dwarf [manzanita](Manzanita "Manzanita") and ceanothus; the unique [Sierra puffball](Calvatia_sculpta "Calvatia sculpta") is also found here. Right below the timberline, in the Hudsonian zone, the whitebark, foxtail, and silver pines grow. At about 10,500 feet (3,200 m), begins the Arctic zone, a treeless region whose flora include a number of wildflowers, including [Sierra primrose](Primula_suffrutescens "Primula suffrutescens"), [yellow columbine](Aquilegia_flavescens "Aquilegia flavescens"), [alpine buttercup](Ranunculus "Ranunculus"), and [alpine shooting star](Dodecatheon_alpinum "Dodecatheon alpinum").[[168]](California#cite_note-California:_flora_and_fauna-170)[[170]](California#cite_note-Life_Zones_of_the_Central_Sierra_Nevada-172)

**Florida** is a [state](U.S._state "U.S. state") in the [Southeastern](Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States") region of the [United States](United_States "United States"), bordered to the west by the [Gulf of Mexico](Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico"); <Alabama> to the northwest; [Georgia](Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)") to the north; the <Bahamas> and [Atlantic Ocean](Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") to the east; and the [Straits of Florida](Straits_of_Florida "Straits of Florida") and <Cuba> to the south. It is the only state that borders both the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean. With a population exceeding 21 million, it is the [third-most populous state in the nation](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_population "List of U.S. states and territories by population") and ranks [eighth in population density](List_of_states_and_territories_of_the_United_States_by_population_density "List of states and territories of the United States by population density") as of 2020. It spans 65,758 square miles (170,310 km2), ranking [22nd in area](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_area "List of U.S. states and territories by area") among the 50 states. The [Miami metropolitan area](Miami_metropolitan_area "Miami metropolitan area"), anchored by the cities of <Miami>, [Fort Lauderdale](Fort_Lauderdale%2C_Florida "Fort Lauderdale, Florida"), and [West Palm Beach](West_Palm_Beach%2C_Florida "West Palm Beach, Florida"), is the state's largest [metropolitan area](Metropolitan_statistical_area "Metropolitan statistical area") with a population of 6.138 million, and the state's most-populous city is [Jacksonville](Jacksonville%2C_Florida "Jacksonville, Florida") with a population of 949,611. Florida's other major population centers include [Tampa Bay](Tampa_Bay_area "Tampa Bay area"), [Orlando](Orlando%2C_Florida "Orlando, Florida"), [Cape Coral](Cape_Coral%2C_Florida "Cape Coral, Florida"), and the state capital of [Tallahassee](Tallahassee%2C_Florida "Tallahassee, Florida").

Various [Native American groups](Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") have inhabited Florida for at least 14,000 years. In 1513, Spanish explorer [Juan Ponce de León](Juan_Ponce_de_Le%C3%B3n "Juan Ponce de León") became the first known European to make landfall, calling the region *La Florida* ([la floˈɾiða]) for its lush greenery and the <Easter> season (*Pascua Florida* in Spanish). Florida subsequently became the first area in the continental U.S. to be permanently settled by Europeans, with the Spanish colony of [St. Augustine](St._Augustine%2C_Florida "St. Augustine, Florida"), founded in 1565, being the oldest continuously inhabited city. Florida was repeatedly contested by [Spain](Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") and [Great Britain](Kingdom_of_Great_Britain "Kingdom of Great Britain") before being [ceded to the U.S.](Adams%E2%80%93On%C3%ADs_Treaty "Adams–Onís Treaty") in 1819; it was admitted as the [27th state](List_of_U.S._states_by_date_of_admission_to_the_Union "List of U.S. states by date of admission to the Union") on March 3, 1845. Florida was the principal location of the [Seminole Wars](Seminole_Wars "Seminole Wars") (1816–1858), the longest and most extensive of the [Indian Wars](American_Indian_Wars "American Indian Wars") in U.S. history. The state seceded from [the Union](Union_(American_Civil_War) "Union (American Civil War)") on January 10, 1861, becoming one of the seven original [Confederate States](Confederate_States_of_America "Confederate States of America"), and was readmitted to the Union after the [Civil War](American_Civil_War "American Civil War") on June 25, 1868.

Since the mid-20th century, Florida has experienced rapid demographic and economic growth. [Its economy](Economy_of_Florida "Economy of Florida"), with a [gross state product](Gross_state_product "Gross state product") (GSP) of $1.4 trillion, is the [fourth-largest of any U.S. state](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_GDP "List of U.S. states and territories by GDP") and the 16th-largest in the world; the main sectors are [tourism](Tourism "Tourism"), [hospitality](Hospitality_industry "Hospitality industry"), [agriculture](Agriculture "Agriculture"), real estate, and [transportation](Transportation_in_Florida "Transportation in Florida"). Florida is world-renowned for its [beach resorts](Beach_resort "Beach resort"), [amusement parks](Amusement_park "Amusement park"), warm and sunny climate, and nautical recreation; attractions such as [Walt Disney World](Walt_Disney_World "Walt Disney World"), the [Kennedy Space Center](Kennedy_Space_Center "Kennedy Space Center"), and [Miami Beach](Miami_Beach%2C_Florida "Miami Beach, Florida") draw tens of millions of visitors annually. Florida has attracted or inspired some of the most prominent American writers, including [Ernest Hemingway](Ernest_Hemingway "Ernest Hemingway"), [Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings](Marjorie_Kinnan_Rawlings "Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings"), and [Tennessee Williams](Tennessee_Williams "Tennessee Williams"), and continues to attract celebrities and athletes, particularly in [golf](Golf "Golf"), [tennis](Tennis "Tennis"), [auto racing](Auto_racing "Auto racing"), and [water sports](List_of_water_sports "List of water sports"). Florida has been considered a [battleground state](Swing_state "Swing state") in [American presidential elections](United_States_presidential_election "United States presidential election"), particularly those in [2000](2000_United_States_presidential_election "2000 United States presidential election"), [2016](2016_United_States_presidential_election "2016 United States presidential election"), and [2020](2020_United_States_presidential_election "2020 United States presidential election").

About two-thirds of Florida occupies a peninsula between the [Gulf of Mexico](Gulf_of_Mexico "Gulf of Mexico") and the [Atlantic Ocean](Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"). It has the [longest coastline](List_of_U.S._states_by_coastline "List of U.S. states by coastline") in the [contiguous United States](Contiguous_United_States "Contiguous United States"), spanning approximately 1,350 miles (2,170 km), not including its many [barrier islands](Barrier_island "Barrier island"). Florida has 4,510 islands that are ten acres (4.0 hectares) or larger in area, the second-largest of any state after <Alaska>. Much of Florida is at or near sea level, and is characterized by [sedimentary](Sediment "Sediment") soil. Florida is the flattest state in the country, with the [lowest high point](List_of_U.S._states_by_elevation "List of U.S. states by elevation") of any U.S. state, at just 345 feet (105 meters).

Florida's climate varies from [subtropical](Subtropical "Subtropical") in the north to [tropical](Tropical "Tropical") in the south. It is the only state besides <Hawaii> to have a [tropical climate](Tropical_climate "Tropical climate"), and is the only continental state with both a tropical climate, located at the southern portion of the state, and a [coral reef](Coral_reef "Coral reef"). Florida has several unique ecosystems, including [Everglades National Park](Everglades_National_Park "Everglades National Park"), the largest tropical wilderness in the U.S. and among the largest in the Americas. Unique wildlife include the [American alligator](American_alligator "American alligator"), [American crocodile](American_crocodile "American crocodile"), [American flamingo](American_flamingo "American flamingo"), [Roseate spoonbill](Roseate_spoonbill "Roseate spoonbill"), [Florida panther](Florida_panther "Florida panther"), [bottlenose dolphin](Common_bottlenose_dolphin "Common bottlenose dolphin"), and [manatee](West_Indian_manatee "West Indian manatee"). The [Florida Reef](Florida_Reef "Florida Reef") is the only living [coral barrier reef](Coral_reef "Coral reef") in the continental United States, and the third-largest coral barrier reef system in the world, after the [Great Barrier Reef](Great_Barrier_Reef "Great Barrier Reef") and the [Belize Barrier Reef](Belize_Barrier_Reef "Belize Barrier Reef").

## History

Main article: [History of Florida](History_of_Florida "History of Florida")

People, known as <Paleo-Indians>, entered Florida at least 14,000 years ago.[[12]](Florida#cite_note-13) By the 16th century, the earliest time for which there is a historical record, major [groups of people](Indigenous_peoples_of_Florida#Early_modern_period "Indigenous peoples of Florida") living in Florida included the <Apalachee> of the [Florida Panhandle](Florida_Panhandle "Florida Panhandle"), the <Timucua> of northern and central Florida, the [Ais](Ais_people "Ais people") of the central Atlantic coast, and the <Calusa> of southwest Florida.[[13]](Florida#cite_note-14)

### European arrival

Main articles: [New Spain](New_Spain "New Spain"), [Spanish Florida](Spanish_Florida "Spanish Florida"), [French and Indian War](French_and_Indian_War "French and Indian War"), [Treaty of Paris (1763)](Treaty_of_Paris_(1763) "Treaty of Paris (1763)"), [West Florida](West_Florida "West Florida"), [East Florida](East_Florida "East Florida"), [Indian Reserve (1763)](Indian_Reserve_(1763) "Indian Reserve (1763)"), [American Revolutionary War](American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"), [Gulf Coast campaign](Gulf_Coast_campaign "Gulf Coast campaign"), [Treaty of Paris (1783)](Treaty_of_Paris_(1783) "Treaty of Paris (1783)"), and [Spanish West Florida](Spanish_West_Florida "Spanish West Florida")

Florida was the first region of what is now the [contiguous United States](Contiguous_United_States "Contiguous United States") to be visited and settled by Europeans. The earliest known European explorers came with the Spanish [conquistador](Conquistador "Conquistador") [Juan Ponce de León](Juan_Ponce_de_Le%C3%B3n "Juan Ponce de León"). Ponce de León spotted and landed on the peninsula on April 2, 1513. He named it *[La Florida](Spanish_Florida "Spanish Florida")* in recognition of the verdant landscape and because it was the <Easter> season, which the <Spaniards> called *[Pascua Florida](Pascua_Florida "Pascua Florida")* (Festival of Flowers). The following day they came ashore to seek information and take possession of this new land.[[14]](Florida#cite_note-Steigman2005-15)[[15]](Florida#cite_note-Names_on_the_Land:_A_Historical_Account_of_Place-Naming_in_the_United_States-16) The story that he was searching for the [Fountain of Youth](Fountain_of_Youth "Fountain of Youth") is mythical and appeared only long after his death.[[16]](Florida#cite_note-17)

In May 1539, Conquistador [Hernando de Soto](Hernando_de_Soto "Hernando de Soto") skirted the coast of Florida, searching for a deep harbor to land. He described a thick wall of red mangroves spread mile after mile, some reaching as high as 70 feet (21 m), with intertwined and elevated roots making landing difficult.[[17]](Florida#cite_note-18) The Spanish introduced [Christianity](Christianity_in_the_United_States "Christianity in the United States"), cattle, horses, sheep, the Castilian language, and more to Florida.[[18]](Florida#cite_note-19) Spain established several settlements in Florida, with varying degrees of success. In 1559, Don [Tristán de Luna y Arellano](Trist%C3%A1n_de_Luna_y_Arellano "Tristán de Luna y Arellano") established a settlement at present-day [Pensacola](Pensacola%2C_Florida "Pensacola, Florida"), making it the first attempted settlement in Florida, but it was mostly abandoned by 1561.

In 1564–1565, there was a French settlement at [Fort Caroline](Fort_Caroline "Fort Caroline"), in present [Duval County](Duval_County%2C_Florida "Duval County, Florida"), which was destroyed by the Spanish.[[19]](Florida#cite_note-Hoffman2004-20)

In 1565, the settlement of [St. Augustine](St._Augustine%2C_Florida "St. Augustine, Florida") (San Agustín) was established under the leadership of admiral and governor [Pedro Menéndez de Avilés](Pedro_Men%C3%A9ndez_de_Avil%C3%A9s "Pedro Menéndez de Avilés"), creating what would become one of the oldest, continuously occupied European settlements in the continental U.S. and establishing the first generation of Floridanos and the [Government of Florida](List_of_colonial_governors_of_Florida "List of colonial governors of Florida").[[20]](Florida#cite_note-21)  Spain maintained strategic control over the region by [converting the local tribes](Spanish_missions_in_Florida "Spanish missions in Florida") to Christianity. The marriage between Luisa de Abrego, a free black domestic servant from Seville, and Miguel Rodríguez, a white Segovian, occurred in 1565 in St. Augustine. It is the first recorded Christian marriage in the continental United States.[[21]](Florida#cite_note-22)

Some Spanish married or had unions with [Pensacola](Pensacola_people "Pensacola people"), [Creek](Muscogee "Muscogee"), or [African](List_of_ethnic_groups_of_Africa "List of ethnic groups of Africa") women, both slave and free, and their descendants created a mixed-race population of [mestizos](Mestizo "Mestizo") and [mulattoes](Mulatto "Mulatto"). The Spanish encouraged [slaves](Slavery_in_the_colonial_United_States "Slavery in the colonial United States") from the [Thirteen Colonies](Thirteen_Colonies "Thirteen Colonies") to come to Florida as a refuge, promising freedom in exchange for conversion to [Catholicism](Catholic_Church "Catholic Church"). [King Charles II of Spain](Charles_II_of_Spain "Charles II of Spain") issued a royal proclamation freeing all slaves who fled to Spanish Florida and accepted conversion and baptism. Most went to the area around [St. Augustine](St._Augustine%2C_Florida "St. Augustine, Florida"), but [escaped slaves](Fugitive_slaves_in_the_United_States "Fugitive slaves in the United States") also reached Pensacola. St. Augustine had mustered an all-black militia unit defending Spanish Florida as early as 1683.[[22]](Florida#cite_note-23)

The geographical area of Spanish claims in *La Florida* diminished with the establishment of English settlements to the north and French claims to the west. English colonists and [buccaneers](Buccaneer "Buccaneer") launched several attacks on St. Augustine in the 17th and 18th centuries, razing the city and its cathedral to the ground several times. ## Geography

Main article: [Geography of Florida](Geography_of_Florida "Geography of Florida")

See also: [List of counties in Florida](List_of_counties_in_Florida "List of counties in Florida"), [List of places in Florida](List_of_places_in_Florida "List of places in Florida"), [List of municipalities in Florida](List_of_municipalities_in_Florida "List of municipalities in Florida"), [List of islands of Florida](List_of_islands_of_Florida "List of islands of Florida"), and [List of Florida state parks](List_of_Florida_state_parks "List of Florida state parks")

Much of Florida is on a peninsula between the Gulf of Mexico, the Atlantic Ocean and the [Straits of Florida](Straits_of_Florida "Straits of Florida"). Spanning two [time zones](Time_zone "Time zone"), it extends to the northwest into a [panhandle](Salient_(geography) "Salient (geography)"), extending along the northern Gulf of Mexico. It is bordered on the north by [Georgia](Georgia_(U.S._state) "Georgia (U.S. state)") and <Alabama>, and on the west, at the end of the panhandle, by Alabama. It is the only state that borders both the Atlantic Ocean and the Gulf of Mexico. Florida also is the southernmost of the 48 contiguous states, <Hawaii> being the only one of the fifty states reaching farther south. Florida is west of the [Bahamas](The_Bahamas "The Bahamas") and 90 miles (140 km) north of <Cuba>. Florida is one of the largest states east of the [Mississippi River](Mississippi_River "Mississippi River"), and only <Alaska> and <Michigan> are larger in water area. The water boundary is 3 nautical miles (3.5 mi; 5.6 km) offshore in the Atlantic Ocean[[72]](Florida#cite_note-NOAA-73) and 9 nautical miles (10 mi; 17 km) offshore in the Gulf of Mexico.[[72]](Florida#cite_note-NOAA-73)

At 345 feet (105 m) [above mean sea level](Above_mean_sea_level "Above mean sea level"), [Britton Hill](Britton_Hill "Britton Hill") is the [highest point](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_elevation "List of U.S. states and territories by elevation") in Florida and the lowest highpoint of any U.S. state.[[73]](Florida#cite_note-Britton-74) Much of the state south of [Orlando](Orlando%2C_Florida "Orlando, Florida") lies at a lower elevation than northern Florida, and is fairly level. Much of the state is at or near sea level. However, some places such as [Clearwater](Clearwater%2C_Florida "Clearwater, Florida") have [promontories](Promontory "Promontory") that rise 50 to 100 ft (15 to 30 m) above the water. Much of Central and North Florida, typically 25 mi (40 km) or more away from the coastline, have rolling hills with elevations ranging from 100 to 250 ft (30 to 76 m). The highest point in peninsular Florida (east and south of the [Suwannee River](Suwannee_River "Suwannee River")), [Sugarloaf Mountain](Sugarloaf_Mountain_(Florida) "Sugarloaf Mountain (Florida)"), is a 312-foot (95 m) peak in [Lake County](Lake_County%2C_Florida "Lake County, Florida").[[74]](Florida#cite_note-Sugarloaf-75) On average, Florida is the flattest state in the United States.[[75]](Florida#cite_note-Megan_Garber-76)

[Lake Okeechobee](Lake_Okeechobee "Lake Okeechobee"), the largest lake in Florida, is the [tenth largest natural freshwater lake](List_of_largest_lakes_of_the_United_States_by_area "List of largest lakes of the United States by area") among the 50 states of the United States and the second-largest natural freshwater lake contained entirely within the [contiguous 48 states](Contiguous_United_States "Contiguous United States"), after [Lake Michigan](Lake_Michigan "Lake Michigan").[[76]](Florida#cite_note-SOFIA_Virtual_Tour-77)

### Climate

Main article: [Climate of Florida](Climate_of_Florida "Climate of Florida")

See also: [List of Florida hurricanes](List_of_Florida_hurricanes "List of Florida hurricanes") and [U.S. state temperature extremes](U.S._state_temperature_extremes "U.S. state temperature extremes")

The climate of Florida is tempered somewhat by the fact that no part of the state is distant from the ocean. North of [Lake Okeechobee](Lake_Okeechobee "Lake Okeechobee"), the prevalent climate is [humid subtropical](Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") ([Köppen](K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): *Cfa*), while areas south of the lake (including the [Florida Keys](Florida_Keys "Florida Keys")) have a true [tropical climate](Tropical_climate "Tropical climate") (Köppen: *Aw*, *Am*, and *Af*).[[77]](Florida#cite_note-Ritter-78) Mean high temperatures for late July are primarily in the low 90s Fahrenheit (32–34 °C). Mean low temperatures for early to mid January range from the low 40s Fahrenheit (4–7 °C) in north Florida to above 60 °F (16 °C) from Miami on southward. With an average daily temperature of 70.7 °F (21.5 °C), it is the warmest state in the U.S.[[78]](Florida#cite_note-79)[[79]](Florida#cite_note-80)

In the summer, high temperatures in the state rarely exceed 100 °F (37.8 °C). Several record cold maxima have been in the 30s °F (−1 to 4 °C) and record lows have been in the 10s (−12 to −7 °C). These temperatures normally extend at most a few days at a time in the northern and central parts of Florida. South Florida, however, rarely encounters below freezing temperatures.[[80]](Florida#cite_note-81) The hottest temperature ever recorded in Florida was 109 °F (43 °C), which was set on June 29, 1931, in [Monticello](Monticello%2C_Florida "Monticello, Florida"). The coldest temperature was −2 °F (−19 °C), on February 13, 1899, just 25 miles (40 km) away, in Tallahassee.[[81]](Florida#cite_note-82)[[82]](Florida#cite_note-83)

Due to its subtropical and tropical climate, Florida rarely receives measurable [snowfall](Snow_in_Florida "Snow in Florida").[[83]](Florida#cite_note-84) However, on rare occasions, a combination of cold moisture and freezing temperatures can result in snowfall in the farthest northern regions like <Jacksonville>, [Gainesville](Gainesville%2C_Florida "Gainesville, Florida") or <Pensacola>. <Frost>, which is more common than [snow](Snow "Snow"), sometimes occurs in the panhandle.[[84]](Florida#cite_note-85) The USDA Plant [hardiness zones](Hardiness_zone "Hardiness zone") for the state range from zone 8a (no colder than 10 °F or −12 °C) in the inland western [panhandle](Florida_panhandle "Florida panhandle") to zone 11b (no colder than 45 °F or 7 °C) in the lower [Florida Keys](Florida_Keys "Florida Keys").[[85]](Florida#cite_note-86) <Fog> also occurs all over the state or climate of Florida.[[86]](Florida#cite_note-87)

The legal name in Florida for a city, town or village is "municipality". In Florida there is no legal difference between towns, villages and cities.[[145]](Florida#cite_note-146)

Florida is a highly urbanized state, with 89 percent of its population living in urban areas in
2000, compared to 79 percent nationally.[[146]](Florida#cite_note-147)

## History

Main article: [History of New York (state)](History_of_New_York_(state) "History of New York (state)")

### Native American history

The [Native American](Native_Americans_in_the_United_States "Native Americans in the United States") tribes in what is now New York were predominantly [Iroquois (Haudenosaunee)](Haudenosaunee "Haudenosaunee") and [Algonquian](Algonquian_peoples "Algonquian peoples").[[10]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-:2-13) [Long Island](Long_Island "Long Island") was divided roughly in half between the Algonquian <Wampanoag> and <Lenape> peoples. The Lenape also controlled most of the region surrounding [New York Harbor](New_York_Harbor "New York Harbor").[[36]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-39) North of the Lenape was a third Algonquian nation, the [Mohicans](Mohican "Mohican"). Starting north of them, from east to west, were two Iroquoian nations: the [Mohawk](Mohawk_people "Mohawk people")—part of the original Iroquois Five Nations, and the <Petun>. South of them, divided roughly along <Appalachia>, were the <Susquehannock> and the [Erie](Erie_(tribe) "Erie (tribe)").[[37]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-40)[[38]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-41)[[39]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-42)[[40]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-43)

Many of the Wampanoag and Mohican peoples were caught up in [King Philip's War](King_Philip's_War "King Philip's War"), a joint effort of many [New England](New_England "New England") tribes to push Europeans off their land. After the death of their leader, Chief Philip <Metacomet>, most of those peoples fled inland, splitting into the <Abenaki> and the [Schaghticoke](Schaghticoke_people "Schaghticoke people"). Many of the Mohicans remained in the region until the 1800s,[[41]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-44) however, a small group known as the Ouabano migrated southwest into [West Virginia](Protohistory_of_West_Virginia "Protohistory of West Virginia") at an earlier time. They may have merged with the <Shawnee>.[[42]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-45)[[43]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-46)

The Mohawk and Susquehannock were the most [militaristic](Militarism "Militarism"). Trying to corner trade with the Europeans, they targeted other tribes. The Mohawk were also known for refusing white settlement on their land and discriminating against any of their people who converted to <Christianity>.[[44]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-47) They posed a major threat to the Abenaki and Mohicans, while the Susquehannock briefly conquered the Lenape in the 1600s. The most devastating event of the century, however, was the [Beaver Wars](Beaver_Wars "Beaver Wars").

From approximately 1640–1680, the Iroquois peoples waged campaigns which extended from modern-day Michigan to Virginia against Algonquian and Siouan tribes, as well as each other. The aim was to control more land for animal [trapping](Trapping "Trapping"),[[45]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-48) a career most natives had turned to in hopes of trading with whites first. This completely changed the ethnography of the region, and most large game was hunted out before whites ever fully explored the land. Still, afterward, the Iroquois Confederacy offered shelter to refugees of the <Mascouten>, Erie, [Chonnonton](Neutral_Nation "Neutral Nation"), <Tutelo>, <Saponi>, and [Tuscarora](Tuscarora_people "Tuscarora people") nations. The Tuscarora became the sixth nation of the Iroquois.

In the 1700s, Iroquoian peoples would take in the remaining Susquehannock of Pennsylvania after they were decimated in the [French and Indian War](French-Indian_War "French-Indian War").[[46]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-49) Most of these other groups assimilated and eventually ceased to exist as separate tribes. Then, after the [American Revolution](American_Revolution "American Revolution"), a large group of Seneca split off and returned to Ohio, becoming known as the <Mingo> Seneca. The current Six Nations of the Iroquois Confederacy include the Seneca, Cayuga, Onondaga, Oneida, Tuscarora and Mohawk. The Iroquois fought for both sides during the [Revolutionary War](American_Revolutionary_War "American Revolutionary War"); afterwards many pro-British Iroquois migrated to Canada. Today, the Iroquois still live in several enclaves across New York and Ontario.[[47]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-50)[[48]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-51)[[49]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-52)[[50]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-53)

Meanwhile, the Lenape formed a close relationship with [William Penn](William_Penn "William Penn"). However, upon Penn's death, his sons managed to take over much of their lands and banish them to Ohio.[[51]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-54) When the U.S. drafted the [Indian Removal Act](Indian_Removal_Act "Indian Removal Act"), the Lenape were further moved to Missouri, whereas their cousins, the Mohicans, were sent to Wisconsin.

Also, in 1778, the United States relocated the [Nanticoke](Nanticoke_people "Nanticoke people") from the [Delmarva Peninsula](Delmarva_Peninsula "Delmarva Peninsula") to the former Iroquois lands south of Lake Ontario, though they did not stay long. Mostly, they chose to migrate into Canada and merge with the Iroquois, although some moved west and merged with the Lenape.[[52]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-55)

## Geography

Main article: [Geography of New York (state)](Geography_of_New_York_(state) "Geography of New York (state)")

The state of New York covers a total area of 54,555 square miles (141,297 km2) and ranks as the [27th largest state by size](List_of_U.S._states_and_territories_by_area "List of U.S. states and territories by area").[[2]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-area-2) The highest elevation in New York is [Mount Marcy](Mount_Marcy "Mount Marcy") in the Adirondacks of [Northern New York](North_Country_(New_York) "North Country (New York)"), at 5,344 feet (1,629 meters) [above sea level](Above_sea_level "Above sea level"); while the state's lowest point is at sea level, on the [Atlantic Ocean](Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean") in [Downstate New York](Downstate_New_York "Downstate New York").[[104]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-usgs-107)

In contrast with New York City's urban landscape, the vast majority of the state's geographic area is dominated by [meadows](Meadow "Meadow"), [forests](Forest "Forest"), rivers, farms, mountains, and lakes. Most of the southern part of the state rests on the [Allegheny Plateau](Allegheny_Plateau "Allegheny Plateau"), which extends from the [southeastern United States](Southeastern_United_States "Southeastern United States") to the [Catskill Mountains](Catskill_Mountains "Catskill Mountains"); the section in the State of New York is known as the [Southern Tier](Southern_Tier "Southern Tier"). The rugged [Adirondack Mountains](Adirondack_Mountains "Adirondack Mountains"), with vast tracts of wilderness, lie west of the [Lake Champlain Valley](Lake_Champlain_Valley "Lake Champlain Valley"). The [Great Appalachian Valley](Great_Appalachian_Valley "Great Appalachian Valley") dominates eastern New York and contains Lake Champlain Valley as its northern half and the [Hudson Valley](Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley") as its southern half within the state. The [Tug Hill](Tug_Hill "Tug Hill") region arises as a [cuesta](Cuesta "Cuesta") east of [Lake Ontario](Lake_Ontario "Lake Ontario").[[105]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-NYS_THComm_Region-108) The state of New York contains a part of the [Marcellus shale](Marcellus_shale "Marcellus shale"), which extends into Ohio and Pennsylvania.[[106]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-frack-109)

*Upstate* and *Downstate* are often used informally to distinguish New York City or its greater metropolitan area from the rest of the State of New York. The placement of a boundary between the two is a matter of great contention.[[107]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-110) Unofficial and loosely defined regions of Upstate New York include from the Southern Tier, which includes many of the counties along the border with Pennsylvania,[[108]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-111) to the [North Country](North_Country_(New_York) "North Country (New York)") region, above or sometimes including parts of the Adirondack region.[[109]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-112)

### Water

#### *Borders*

Of the State of New York's total area, 13.6% consists of water.[[110]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-113) Much of New York's boundaries are in water, as is true for New York City: four of its [five boroughs](Borough_(New_York_City) "Borough (New York City)") are situated on three islands at the mouth of the [Hudson River](Hudson_River "Hudson River"): [Manhattan Island](Manhattan "Manhattan"); [Staten Island](Staten_Island "Staten Island"); and [Long Island](Long_Island "Long Island"), which contains <Brooklyn> and <Queens> at its western end. The state's borders include a water boundary in (clockwise from the west) two [Great Lakes](Great_Lakes "Great Lakes") ([Lake Erie](Lake_Erie "Lake Erie") and [Lake Ontario](Lake_Ontario "Lake Ontario"), which are connected by the [Niagara River](Niagara_River "Niagara River")); the provinces of <Ontario> and <Quebec> in <Canada>, with New York and Ontario sharing the [Thousand Islands](Thousand_Islands "Thousand Islands") [archipelago](Archipelago "Archipelago") within the Saint Lawrence River, while most of its border with Quebec is on land; it shares [Lake Champlain](Lake_Champlain "Lake Champlain") with the [New England](New_England "New England") state of <Vermont>; the New England state of <Massachusetts> has mostly a land border; New York extends into [Long Island Sound](Long_Island_Sound "Long Island Sound") and the [Atlantic Ocean](Atlantic_Ocean "Atlantic Ocean"), sharing a water border with [Rhode Island](Rhode_Island "Rhode Island"), while <Connecticut> has land and sea borders. Except for areas near the [New York Harbor](New_York_Harbor "New York Harbor") and the Upper [Delaware River](Delaware_River "Delaware River"), New York has a mostly land border with two [Mid-Atlantic states](Mid-Atlantic_states "Mid-Atlantic states"), [New Jersey](New_Jersey "New Jersey") and <Pennsylvania>. New York is the only state that includes within its borders parts of the Great Lakes and the Atlantic Ocean.

#### *Drainage*

The [Hudson River](Hudson_River "Hudson River") begins near [Lake Tear of the Clouds](Lake_Tear_of_the_Clouds "Lake Tear of the Clouds") and flows south through the eastern part of the state, without draining Lakes [George](Lake_George_(lake)%2C_New_York "Lake George (lake), New York") or [Champlain](Lake_Champlain "Lake Champlain"). Lake George empties at its north end into Lake Champlain, whose northern end extends into Canada, where it drains into the [Richelieu River](Richelieu_River "Richelieu River") and then ultimately the [Saint Lawrence River](Saint_Lawrence_River "Saint Lawrence River"). The western section of the state is drained by the [Allegheny River](Allegheny_River "Allegheny River") and rivers of the [Susquehanna](Susquehanna_River "Susquehanna River") and [Delaware River](Delaware_River "Delaware River") systems. [Niagara Falls](Niagara_Falls "Niagara Falls") is shared between New York and Ontario as it flows on the Niagara River from Lake Erie to Lake Ontario. The Delaware River Basin Compact, signed in 1961 by New York, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, <Delaware>, and the federal government, regulates the utilization of water of the Delaware system.[[111]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-114)

New York is divided into 62 [counties](County_(United_States) "County (United States)"). Aside from the five counties of New York City, each of these counties is subdivided into [towns](Town#New_York "Town") and [cities](City "City"), incorporated under state law. Towns can contain incorporated [villages](Village "Village") or unincorporated [hamlets](Hamlet_(place)#New_York "Hamlet (place)"). New York City is divided into five [boroughs](Borough_(New_York_City) "Borough (New York City)"), each coterminous with a county. The major cities of the state developed along the key transportation and [trade routes](Trade_route "Trade route") of the early 19th century, including the [Erie Canal](Erie_Canal "Erie Canal") and railroads paralleling it. Today, the [New York Thruway](New_York_Thruway "New York Thruway") acts as a modern counterpart to commercial water routes.[[139]](New_York_(state)#cite_note-142) [Downstate New York](Downstate_New_York "Downstate New York") ([New York City](Geography_of_New_York_City "Geography of New York City"), [Long Island](Long_Island "Long Island"), and the southern portion of the [Hudson Valley](Hudson_Valley "Hudson Valley")) can be considered to form the central core of the [Northeast megalopolis](Northeast_megalopolis "Northeast megalopolis"), an urbanized region stretching from [New Hampshire](New_Hampshire "New Hampshire") to <Virginia>.
